title: How to talk to anyone without feeling AWKWARD | English Small Talk 2

lines.text: If you're learning English and you suck
at small talk,
you're not alone.
Today, I want to help you improve your
English small talk so you can talk to
strangers without feeling nervous or
awkward.
Firstly, we're going to learn what is
the point of small talk. After that, how
to start a conversation [music]
and keep it going. Then, some common
small talk mistakes. And finally, how to
leave without seeming rude.
First and foremost, most small talk
conversations begin with
"Hey, how's it going?"
or
"How are you doing?"
And the answer is usually
"I'm good. How are you?"
"Not bad."
Even if you're feeling shh
we don't mention our problems at this
stage, especially with someone that we
have just met. After my last small talk
video, a lot of people asked me, "Is
small talk fake?"
I want to tell you a little story. So, I
used to work at an Asian company and my
colleagues hardly ever made small talk
with me.
They were much more direct and they got
straight to work.
But, after working together with them
for a while,
I got to know them better.
And that made me realize it's just a
cultural difference. You see, in England
and in other English-speaking countries,
we like to get to know each other a
little bit before getting down to
business.
And once you understand that, then small
talk won't feel fake anymore.
Small talk isn't about sharing important
information or your deepest feelings,
but it is a necessary step to open up
communication between humans.
You're helping the other person feel
comfortable enough to continue the
conversation.
So, the goal is comfort, not perfect
English.
People aren't judging your English as
much as you think they are.
They're mainly asking themselves,
"Do I feel comfortable enough talking to
this person?"
A small grammar mistake is much less
important than showing warmth,
curiosity, and attention.
But, Jay, what if I don't know how to
start a conversation?
[music]
So, after saying, "Hi, how are you?"
or
"How's it going?"
where do you go?
Well, you can use what is already around
you.
So, for example, if you're at a cafe,
you can say,
"Do you come here often?"
"What's your favorite thing on the
menu?"
"What would you recommend?"
"Oh, nice.
I'm going to try that."
Or, if you're at a social event, you can
say things like,
"So, how do you know the host?"
"Do you know many people here?"
"I love your outfit, by the way.
Where did you buy that?"
Okay. So, now we know how to start a
conversation.
What to say after that?
It's useful to think of small talk like
a game of tennis.
In tennis, you hit the ball back and
forth to keep the rally going. In small
talk, we don't have a ball.
But, we do ask questions, and then
answer those questions. And this keeps
the conversation flowing.
Right, you ask a question
and someone is answering. How do you
respond?
The best small talkers do that by
listening attentively,
looking at the speaker, keeping eye
contact,
and having open, relaxed body language.
It's also easy to feel awkward with our
hands. Where do we put them?
You can have your hands in front of you,
behind you,
on your hips,
or in your pockets.
Try not to cross your arms.
This is closed body language.
A really useful tip is to grab a drink.
Have a bottle of water with you.
This will help your hands feel less
awkward, and it will help you feel less
rushed to respond.
You can pause and take a sip before you
speak.
Beyond body language is our facial
expressions. You smile and nod to
encourage them to keep speaking. You can
say things like, "Oh, nice."
"Mhm."
"All right, cool."
"Oh, me too."
And then
you take your turn to speak.
Let's look at a few examples.
Hey, how's it going?
Hey, it's going well, thanks.
How are you doing?
I'm good, thank you.
By the way, I'm Jay.
Nice to meet you, Jay. I'm Tim.
Nice to meet you, Tim.
I'm curious, how do you know the host?
Oh, we know each other from work. I
started working with her a year ago. How
about you?
I met her at our tennis club. We play
doubles together.
Are you into any sports?
Just like anything, we learn by doing.
So, the best way to get better at small
talk is to practice having conversations
daily.
You will naturally get better at it.
If you don't have anyone to practice
with,
you can chat with Jay AI on Sprout on
any role-play situation.
He will ask you questions, keep the
conversation going, so you can get your
daily English practice.
But Jay,
what's a common small talk mistake?
[bell]
A lot of English learners don't know
what to say.
And because of that, you might give very
short answers.
Let's look at an example.
So, Lucy, what genre of books do you
like reading?
I like fiction.
Nice. Me, too.
I usually read non-fiction, but recently
I have been reading some fiction books.
I've been reading a book called The
Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. Have
you read it?
No, I haven't.
Did you notice the problem with Lucy's
answers there?
They were too short.
The problem with short answers is that
it gives less detail for the other
person to ask you questions and to keep
the conversation going. The solution to
that is to
share more.
Give more detail in your answers. Share
your personality.
And remember to ask questions back.
When you share more, you can use what
you said to spark your next question.
Let's look at another example.
So, Lucy, what genre of books do you
like reading?
I like fiction.
I'm really into mystery and crime
novels.
And I love to read them when I go on
holiday.
Are you into crime novels?
I don't tend to read crime fiction.
I usually read non-fiction books, but
I'm curious.
Have you got any recommendations for
crime fiction books?
Yeah,
I just finished the book Thursday Murder
Club by Richard Osman.
I would highly recommend it.
Nice. I think I'll check it out.
What's it about?
What a game of tennis that was.
[laughter]
Why did that conversation between Lucy
and I flow so smoothly?
Simple.
We asked questions and then we gave
details in our answers.
In small talk, if you want to be
interesting,
be interested.
But Jay, how do we leave without being
rude?
If the conversation is going well and
you share things in common,
then you can go from small talk to deep
talk and I'll share more about that in a
future video.
But what if the conversation is a little
dry or what if it's come to its natural
end?
How do you leave without seeming rude?
Well, the solution is some simple exit
lines.
It was really nice chatting with you,
Lucy. I'm going to grab another drink
now, but I'll see you around. I'm just
going to say hi to a few more people
before I leave, but it was nice to chat.
I'm going to get back to my friends now,
but it was nice chatting.
[music]
Now let's recap what we learned in this
video to help it stick in
here.
Firstly, we learned that small talk
isn't fake. It's just a part of our
culture. It helps us create social ease
and build positive relationships with
each other.
Secondly, we learned that to start a
conversation, we can simply use the
environment and the context around us.
Thirdly, we learned that small talk is
like a game of tennis. We ask questions
and then we respond.
We also learned the importance of open
body language, smiling, and
positive facial expressions. We learned
that giving very short answers doesn't
give enough information for the other
person to ask us questions and keep the
conversation going. And finally, we
learned how to end a conversation using
simple exit lines.
So guys, it was lovely chatting with
you. I'm just going to grab a drink, so
I'll catch you in a bit. Yeah.
